result.summary: Pausanias describes Heraea in Arcadia, its temples, its athlete Damaretus, and its borders with Elis. He then covers Aliphera with its Athene cult, and the sites of Melaeneae and Buphagium.

scenes.title: Heraea and its borders
scenes.summary: Heraea's founder, buildings and temples are described, along with Damaretus and the disputed boundary with Elis, marked by the tomb of Coroebus.

scenes.title: Aliphera and Athene
scenes.summary: Aliphera is reached over a mountain. Its people claim Athene was born there and sacrifice to Muiagrus to be free of flies.

scenes.title: Melaeneae and Buphagium
scenes.summary: Melaeneae is deserted and flooded, and Buphagium lies above it, where the Buphagus rises and marks a boundary.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Zeus meaning roughly 'of childbed', from his giving birth to Athene.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable custom of sacrificing to the Flycatcher to be rid of flies.

analysis.text: Local claims shape the account: Aliphera claims Athene's birth and Elis and Arcadia dispute a boundary.
The Olympic victor Coroebus and Iphitus's refounding of the games show how Greeks dated their past through athletic records.

fun_facts.text: Coroebus of Elis is traditionally recorded as the first Olympic victor, in 776 BC.

language_notes.text: Polites means 'of the citizen'; Auxites means 'the increaser' (giver of growth). Both are cult titles of Dionysus.
Orgies here means secret ritual rites, not the modern sense of the word.
The race in heavy armour was the hoplite race, run by competitors carrying shield and armour.
A stade is a Greek measure of length, roughly 600 feet or about 180 metres.
Iphitus of Elis traditionally revived the Olympic games; Coroebus is recorded as the first Olympic victor, in the footrace.
Lecheates is a title apparently meaning 'of the childbed', hence Zeus 'who gave birth' to Athene.
Tritonis recalls the Triton, a river or lake linked to Athene's birth in other traditions; Aliphera claims that story for itself.
Muiagrus is Greek for 'fly-catcher', a hero or god invoked to keep flies away.

context_notes.text: Lycaon was the legendary early king of Arcadia, and many Arcadian towns are said to be named for his sons.
Megalopolis was founded around 370 BC, and many small Arcadian towns lost people to it.
Æsculapius is the god of healing.

literary_notes.text: The fly-averting rite is told with gentle detachment, and the sacrifice to a minor power comes before the main god.
Towns named after Lycaon's sons recur, reinforcing Arcadia's founding genealogy.
